one_liner: Research C++14 PQ search engine whose AVX2 scan uses 4-bit sub-quantizers and pshufb tables; about 3.8x faster scans than scalar ADC.
what_it_does: A small product-quantization search toolkit: executables build flat or inverted-file (IVF) databases from PQ/OPQ codebooks learned elsewhere, add .fvecs/.bvecs vectors, and query them with either conventional ADC (db_query) or Quick ADC (db_query_4), printing Recall@r and per-stage times. It is not a library; reuse means lifting scanner_4 and scan_avx_4 (simd_scan.hpp, simd_layout.hpp, query_common.hpp), which expect 16x4 or 32x4-bit codes (64 or 128 bits per vector) re-laid out in blocks of 16.
how_it_is_fast: With 16-centroid (4-bit) sub-quantizers every distance table has 16 entries, so after quantizing the float tables to int8 it fits one 128-bit register. Codes are transposed into 16-vector blocks; scan_avx_4 does two pshufb lookups per byte (low and high nibble) with saturating int8 adds, two sub-quantizer rows per 256-bit register, then compares the 16 sums against the int8 heap bound with a movemask and pushes only survivors. The quantization range comes from a scalar float scan of a small 'keep' fraction of each probed cell (0.213% in the README run), which sets qmax to the current top-r bound.
when_to_use: IVF-ADC search with many small cells and multiple assignment (the README run probes 24 of 256 cells on SIFT1M), where PQ Fast Scan's per-partition grouping cannot be used.
64-bit (16x4) or 128-bit (32x4) codes on x86-64 with AVX2, when you accept a small recall loss for about 4x faster code scans.
Recall@100-style workloads where the true neighbour only has to land somewhere in a 100-item candidate list that a later stage re-ranks.
As a compact reference for the 4-bit pshufb fast-scan kernel that Faiss later productised.
when_not_to_use: When you need exact ADC distances or a precise top-1: results are ranked by 8-bit quantized sums with no float re-ranking pass in db_query_4, on top of the 4-bit quantizer loss (Recall@100 0.9426 vs 0.9646 for 8x8 OPQ in the README run).
8-bit codes or code sizes other than 16x4 and 32x4: get_simd_scan_func_epi8 exits on anything else.
CPUs without AVX2 or non-x86 targets (config.h hard-defines AVX2; -march=native).
Production deployments: three commits, abandoned since 2019, no library target or tests; Faiss IndexIVFPQFastScan (which credits the same authors' fast-scan work) is the maintained route.
Inner-product or other metrics with negative table entries: negative entries are clamped to zero before quantization.

integration.dependencies: sequential (single-threaded) BLAS such as OpenBLAS 0.2.19 built by getdeps.sh, OpenCV core, Cereal 1.2.2; codebooks must be learned with an external tool (arbabenko/Quantizations) and converted by convert-quantizer.py
integration.min_toolchain: C++14, g++ 5.4 or newer, CMake 3.2 (CMakeLists) although the README says 2.8; -O3 -march=native -ffast-math -fopenmp -Werror
integration.platforms: x86-64 Linux with AVX and AVX2 (tested on Intel Haswell, Broadwell and Skylake per README)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; each nns_engine owns its table, residual and assignment buffers and query_scan clamps the caller's tables in place, so use one engine per thread; OpenMP is used only when building databases
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: same IVF structure and code size as ADC, but it needs 4-bit codebooks, a re-laid-out copy of each cell and a tuned keep parameter, and returns int8-quantized distances

gotchas: The keep fraction must give at least r scalar-scanned codes across the probed cells, otherwise qmax stays at FLT_MAX and db_query_4 exits with 'Max quantization bound too high. Try larger keep value.'; the README recommends keep between 0.05% and 1%, and -k is given in percent.

Tail handling in scan_avx_4: the last block of each cell is padded with copies of the cell's last code and padded lanes are not masked; bh_push clamps their index to the last code, so that code can enter the top-r list up to 16 times, displacing real candidates (minor effect on recall, none on timing).

The README comparison changes two variables at once: ADC scans 8x8 OPQ codes while Quick ADC scans 16x4 OPQ codes (same 64-bit size, lower recall). Both use batches of 32 queries; scan_us is averaged over the whole query set and includes Quick ADC's scalar keep pass and table quantization.
Dataset, slide and poster links on assets.xion345.info no longer resolve (issue #1 reports broken links; the host did not resolve in this session).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over its sibling PQ Fast Scan when the database is an IVF index with many small cells or you can use 4-bit codes; PQ Fast Scan returns exact 8x8-bit ADC results but only pays off on large, re-laid-out partitions. No other catalogued SIMD library targets PQ distance scans.
verified_claims_summary: README example on SIFT1M with an IVF index of 256 cells, 24 cells probed and r = 100: the authors' scalar ADC over 8x8 OPQ codes scans in 323 us per query (Recall@100 0.9646) versus 86 us for Quick ADC over 16x4 OPQ codes with keep 0.213% (Recall@100 0.9426), about 3.8x (derived from page data); the README states 4-6x and the ICMR 2017 paper abstract 3-6x (snippet only). Built with g++ 5.4+ -O3 -march=native -ffast-math; tested on Haswell, Broadwell and Skylake, with no CPU model given for these numbers.
status_note: Abandoned since 2019-05-31 (3 commits, 27 stars) but Clear-BSD-licensed research code with a self-contained AVX2 kernel; the authors' later Quicker ADC (technicolor-research/faiss-quickeradc, AVX-512, non-4-bit codes) and Faiss's FastScan indexes supersede it.
